finding: The only isolation §6.1 permits changes two of the three inputs its own equality property holds fixed. §6.1 states the property as "For a fixed spec, corpus and state directory…" and then narrows the mechanism to one option: `engine.ReviewStateDir` derives the state directory from the spec's own path "with no flag or environment override, so relocating the state means relocating the spec". Measured on the shipped binary: a bare copy of `spec/0.37.0.md` in an empty directory, `TP_*` cleared, emits roles `implementer, tester, architect` at `review_loop.round: 1` — the embedded 3-role default corpus, not this repository's 4-role `.tp/reviewers/` corpus, because `ResolveActiveCorpus` resolves relative to the tree the command runs in, not to the spec. So the prescribed relocation silently swaps the corpus and resets the round, and an emission compared under it is not the emission the release ships. §6.1 says it "prescribes none" and fixes the outcome instead, but the one sentence it does state about mechanism is the one that breaks the property.
suggestion: State the third input explicitly: the isolation must relocate the spec *together with* its `.tp-review/<base>/` state directory and must run with the repository's `.tp/` (corpus and config) still resolvable — otherwise `corpus` and `round`, which the §6.1 property names as held fixed, are not fixed. Alternatively drop "corpus" from the property and say which corpus the tests run against.

finding: This round moved `--verify` from the refused column to the legal column of §4.2.2's table, and §6.3 test 11 — which was not rewritten — still routes it the old way: "`--verify` is not in this list — it is in test 10's, per §4.2." Test 10 iterates "each refusing mode in §4.2.2's table", and §4.2.2's refused column for `tp review` is now `--merge`, `--record`, `--status`, `--report`, `--resolve`, `--resolve-all` — `--verify` is not in it. So three things are wrong at once: (a) test 11 asserts the opposite of the normative table, telling an implementer that `--verify` + `--role` is a refusal case; (b) `--verify` + `--role` is now covered by NO test at all — it is excluded from test 11 by name and absent from test 10's iteration set — and it is the single mode §4.2.2 spent its whole new paragraph re-classifying; (c) the citation "per §4.2" points at a section that says nothing about `--verify` (the mode table is §4.2.2's). An implementer who follows test 11 writes a suite asserting exit 2 for `tp review <spec> --verify --role verifier`, which ships the behaviour §4.2.2 explicitly dropped.
suggestion: Rewrite test 11's last sentence to include `--verify` in the legal-mode list: "`--role` with `--perspective`, with `--diff-from` and with `--verify` exits 0 and emits one prompt. `tp review` only; `tp audit` has none of those flags." Delete the "it is in test 10's, per §4.2" pointer. If test 11's per-mode role names are still open (§6.3's existing round-6 finding), name `verifier` for `--verify` here as §4.2.2 already does.

finding: Test 19's rewritten predicate is not machine-decidable, so the test cannot be written. It requires the suite to "split both instructions into sentences, and require that every sentence present without `--role` and absent with it directs an action a single-prompt caller cannot take, while every sentence kept is one it can." Classifying a natural-language sentence as "directs an action a single-prompt caller cannot take" is a semantic judgement; a Go test can only decide it against an enumerated set of sentences or directive keywords — which is exactly the list form §4.2.3 rejects ("The rule is a property, not a list of sentences to delete") and which test 19's own paragraph rejects a second time ("A draft enumerated the forbidden directives instead"). The spec therefore forbids the only construction that satisfies it. An implementer has to either smuggle the list back in under another name or write an assertion that passes on any partition, which is the same tautology test 16's paragraph rejects for a different test.
suggestion: Replace the semantic predicate with a mechanical one the emitter can guarantee. Since `buildReviewLoopInstruction` assembles the key from nine assignment sites, tag each site with a boolean at the source — e.g. `singlePromptSafe` — and make test 19 assert the derived property: with `--role`, the instruction equals the concatenation of exactly the sites whose tag is true; without `--role`, it equals the concatenation of all sites. That is derived from the code rather than from a written list, keeps §4.2.3's rule as the *authoring* rule for the tag, and is decidable.

finding: Round 9 rewrote §4.2.2 to move `--verify` into the legal column and to ground legality on a rule with "no exceptions" — `--role` is legal wherever prompts are emitted. Measured on the shipped binary against a copy of this spec (TP_* cleared, isolated tree): `--perspective documentation` emits 1 prompt (`documentation-planner`, 3,760 B), `--perspective testing` 1 (`test-planner`, 3,315 B), `--verify` 1 (`verifier`, 2,098 B). In every one of those modes `--role` can only return the single prompt the mode already returns, so it removes zero bytes — against the 90.6% §4.3 books, which is a default-mode figure. So five of the six `tp review` configurations §4.2.2 now calls legal deliver none of the release's only measured benefit, and the section prices none of them at zero. What the uniformity buys instead is cost the spec does pay: §6.3 test 10's two-way partition, test 11, and §4.2.1's exit-0-with-empty-`prompts[]` branch made reachable in modes whose only selectable name (`documentation-planner`/`test-planner`/`verifier`) the spec never prints — so an agent must first invoke without `--role` to learn the name, a round-trip strictly more expensive than omitting the flag. All three of those prompts also carry `output_path: ""`, so by §2.3's own predicate the prompt `--role` selects there carries neither of this release's two clauses; §4.2.2's "the same behaviour as everywhere else" is false on the release's other half.
suggestion: Restate the criterion as reduction rather than as emission: `--role` is refused where the mode emits fewer than two prompts. That is mechanical, has no exceptions, and — unlike the draft criterion §4.2.2 rejected ("a flag that cannot change the output") — it condemns `--verify` and the one-prompt perspectives consistently rather than condemning modes the table calls legal. Shrinking the legal set to {default, --diff-from} also deletes test 11 and half of test 10's partition. If uniformity is kept instead, say in §4.2.2 that legality in one-prompt modes is worth 0 bytes and is bought for rule-shape alone, and print the three role names the spec currently withholds.

finding: §4.2.2's new closing sentence asserts that the one-prompt modes need no special rule — "`--role` is legal wherever prompts are emitted, and in a one-prompt mode it selects that prompt or exits 0 empty by §4.2.1's rule, which is the same behaviour as everywhere else" — and §4.2.1's rule cannot reach those modes. §4.2.1's exit-0 branch is conditioned on an output the mode does not produce: it requires exit 0 "with `prompts: []` and the role's own entry present in `skipped_roles`, carrying the reason tp already computes". Verified in the tree: `skipped_roles` is assembled only on the emitting paths — `runReview` (internal/cli/review.go:579-585, from buildReviewPrompts' `skipped`) and `runAudit` (audit.go:333-373) — and the struct field is `*[]engine.SkippedRole` with `json:"skipped_roles,omitempty"`. `--verify` is dispatched to `runReviewVerify` (review_verify.go), which never sets the field, so the key is absent from the payload entirely. `engine/skipped.go` also only ever appends corpus role ids plus `regression`, so `verifier` and `test-planner` can never be members even where the key exists. Consequently `tp review <spec> --verify --role architect` satisfies neither branch: `architect` is in the corpus so it is not "a name tp recognises nowhere" (no exit 2), and there is no `skipped_roles` entry for it (no exit 0 as specified). §4.2.2 therefore books as settled the trichotomy hole that is still open at §4.2, and does it for the exact modes the paragraph was written to legalise.
suggestion: Either (a) weaken §4.2.1's exit-0 branch so the `skipped_roles` entry is emitted-if-computed rather than required — 'exits 0 with `prompts: []`, and where tp computes a skip reason for the name that reason is echoed in `skipped_roles`' — which makes the branch reachable in every mode; or (b) state in §4.2.2 that in a one-prompt mode a non-matching recognised name exits 0 with an empty `prompts[]` and no `skipped_roles` entry, and say so instead of claiming it is 'the same behaviour as everywhere else'. Either way §6.3 needs a case for a corpus role name passed to `--verify`, since neither test 10 nor test 11 reaches it today.

finding: §6.1 now states the isolation requirement as 'The isolation must preserve state behaviour and relocate it' and then hands the outcome to one assertion: 'spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ under the repository root are byte-identical before and after the suite runs. §6.4 test 18 owns that assertion.' Only the RELOCATE half has an owner. Test 18 asserts that nothing was written — a suite that discards review state entirely (the `--no-state`-shaped failure §6.1's own preceding paragraph describes, 'pass while measuring a machine that had been switched off') passes test 18 perfectly, because a machine that reads no state writes none either. So the condition §6.1 calls out as the dangerous one is the one with no test, and the tests that depend on it silently degrade rather than fail: test 7 needs a round where regression IS emitted and a round 1 where it is not, test 9 needs a `no-baseline` fixture, test 17 needs 'a round where regression is emitted', and test 14 — the release gate — buys its whole justification from §7's claim that the repository corpus 'exercises both sides of the one skip reason that is round-dependent'. Every one of those reduces to a round-1 emission, and passes, if the relocated state is empty.
suggestion: Give the preserve half an owner with a discriminating assertion, e.g. a numbered test that runs one emission under the suite's isolation and asserts the panel is the round-dependent one — `regression` present with a non-`no-baseline` state and absent at round 1, and the round number in `review_loop.round` equal to the fixture's — so a suite that relocated the state without carrying it fails loudly instead of reporting green.

finding: Test 4's "derived, not enumerated" construction cannot be executed for three of its four values. It says "the test emits from every value `--perspective` accepts (`documentation`, `testing`, `code-audit`, `regression`) plus `--verify`". Measured against the shipped binary: `--perspective documentation` exits 2 with `--docs-path is required when --perspective=documentation`; `--perspective testing` exits 2 with `--test-path is required`; `--perspective code-audit` exits 2 with `requires at least one --affected-files`. Only `regression` emits from the flag alone. So iterating the validated set does not produce four emissions — it produces one emission and three exit-2s, and the spec never names the docs directory, test directory or affected-file list the other three need. The same gap disables §6.3 test 11 ("`--role` with `--perspective` … exits 0 and emits one prompt"), which has no legal `--perspective` value it can use without inventing those arguments.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §6.2 test 4 (and reference it from test 11) naming the companion arguments the derivation must supply per value — e.g. the suite passes the relocated tree's own directory for `--docs-path` and `--test-path` and a single file from it for `--affected-files`. Keep the derivation over `review.go`'s validated set; only the argument-per-value mapping needs to be stated, because that is the part the code does not carry.

finding: Round 9's only new normative surface is covered by no test and is contradicted by the test section. §4.2.2's table now lists `--verify` in `tp review`'s legal column. Test 10 iterates "each refusing mode in §4.2.2's table", which no longer contains `--verify`, so test 10 does not touch it. Test 11 — the only other `--role`-combination test — then excludes it in terms: "`--verify` is not in this list — it is in test 10's". Both statements were true before round 9 and neither is now, so `--role` + `--verify` is the single combination this round added and the only legal combination with zero coverage. The economy cost is the one this project keeps paying: a flag combination an agent may legally form, whose behaviour no assertion pins, is a round-trip to the code or to a trial invocation — the round-trip tp exists to remove — and §4.2.1 routes the most likely such invocation (`--verify --role implementer`, a recognised corpus name the mode does not emit) to exit 0 with `prompts: []`, i.e. a silent no-work success indistinguishable on the exit code from a served request.
suggestion: Delete test 11's `--verify` sentence and add `--verify` to test 11's own legal-combination list, asserting both branches that §4.2.2 now promises there: `--role verifier --verify --findings <f>` emits that one prompt, and `--role <a corpus role>` with `--verify` exits 0 with an empty `prompts[]` and the role echoed in `skipped_roles`. If §4.2.2 instead adopts the fewer-than-two-prompts criterion, the same edit is a one-word restoration of `--verify` to test 10's list — but one of the two edits has to be made this round, because the current pair of sentences is false either way.

finding: Test 12 asserts the delta 'inside each `prompts[].prompt`', a universal over the payload's entries, while §2.3 makes clause emission conditional: 'The clauses are appended to every prompt whose `output_path` is non-empty, and to no other.' The two agree only if every entry of the DEFAULT payload has a non-empty `output_path`, and the spec never says whether the auto-appended `regression` entry does — the one entry §4 says is 62% of the payload. The document hints both ways: §4.1 says regression's prompt is 'assigned to none, and produce[s] no output file', which reads as no output path; §6.2 test 4 builds its empty-`output_path` set from `--perspective` values including `regression`, which is a different invocation and settles nothing about the auto-appended entry. Three tests need the answer and would be written differently under each: test 12's 'each', test 5's exact 467 (measured on which entry?), and test 4's 'Neither clause appears in any prompt whose output_path is empty' — if the default payload contains such a prompt, test 4's derived set was supposed to catch it and its derivation does not reach the default mode at all.
suggestion: State in §2.3 whether the auto-appended `regression` entry carries an `output_path`, and therefore whether it receives the clauses. Then either qualify test 12 to 'each prompts[].prompt whose output_path is non-empty' or, if regression does carry one, say so and keep the universal — and extend test 4's derived set to include the default mode's entries so the classification is decided where the payload actually is.

finding: Test 14 and test 18 are jointly unsatisfiable against the live tree, and test 14 is the release gate. Test 14 runs test 13 "against every spec in `spec/` the repository can emit prompts for"; §6.1's first sentence states that `tp review <spec>` and `tp audit <spec>` "take the round's snapshot as a side effect". Of §7's own 22 version specs, 15 have a directory under `spec/.tp-review/` (verified: 15 dirs) and 7 do not — so emitting for those 7 creates new state directories. Test 18 asserts `spec/.tp-review/` hashes identically before and after, "as a directory hash, not per file, so a file the suite creates fails it as loudly as a file it edits". The gate therefore fails test 18 by construction, and the only escape §6.1 names — relocating the spec — puts every one of the 22 at round 1, which destroys the single property §7 says breadth buys ("exercises both sides of the one skip reason that is round-dependent (`regression`, skipped `no-baseline` at round 1 and emitted after)").
suggestion: Resolve the two tests against each other in §6.1 rather than leaving it to the implementer: state that the suite relocates each spec together with its recorded `spec/.tp-review/<base>/`, so the copies keep their round numbers and the 15/7 split survives; then test 18's assertion is about the repository tree, which the suite never touches, and test 14's breadth is preserved. If that is too expensive, say which of the two the gate gives up.

finding: §4.2.2 was rewritten this round to move `--verify` into the LEGAL column ('The split is mechanical and has no exceptions... in a one-prompt mode it selects that prompt or exits 0 empty by §4.2.1's rule'), but §6.3 test 11 still carries the sentence written against the old table: '`--verify` is not in this list — it is in test 10's, per §4.2.' Test 10 is 'each refusing mode in §4.2.2's table exits 2'. So the two normative statements the implementer must satisfy are: §4.2.2 says `tp review <spec> --verify --role <name>` is legal, and test 11 says it belongs to the test that asserts exit 2. Two engineers write opposite tests from the same document. The consequence is worse than the contradiction: with `--verify` out of §4.2.2's refused column and explicitly excluded from test 11, NO numbered test in §6 exercises `--role` with `--verify` at all — the one mode §4.2.2 spends a whole paragraph justifying is the one mode the suite does not cover. The trailing anchor '§4.2' is also stale: §4.2 now contains no table.
suggestion: Delete test 11's third sentence and add `--verify` to test 11's legal list, with the name pinned (§4.2.2 and earlier rounds establish the emitted role is `verifier`), so the assertion reads: `--role verifier` with `--verify` exits 0 and emits that one prompt, and `--role <any other name>` with `--verify` exits 0 with `prompts: []` per §4.2.1. Repoint the anchor to §4.2.2.

finding: Test 16 says "execute its `brief_command` and assert exit 0", but `brief_command` is a command *string* beginning with the bare word `tp` (§4.2.3 fixes its new form as `tp review <spec> --role <id>`), and the spec states no rule for which binary that word resolves to. Inside `go test` it resolves through `PATH` to the installed release, which is the one binary guaranteed not to have `--role` — so on the day the test is written it fails with an unknown-flag error unrelated to the change, and after the release ships it passes while exercising a tree that is not the one under test. The same word appears in test 15's "end-to-end through `tp run --dry-run`". §6.1 is explicit that both sides of its equality "come from the same tree"; test 16 is the one assertion in §6 that leaves the tree unnamed.
suggestion: Add the condition to §6.1 alongside the other two: any test that executes an emitted command string runs it against a binary built from the tree under test (e.g. `go build -o <tmp>/tp ./cmd/tp` with `<tmp>` prepended to `PATH`, or the string's first token substituted), and never against `PATH`'s `tp`. That is a property, not a harness — it says which tree, and leaves the construction to the task.

finding: Test 19 replaces last round's enumerated list with a derived predicate that no test can evaluate: 'split both instructions into sentences, and require that every sentence present without `--role` and absent with it directs an action a single-prompt caller cannot take, while every sentence kept is one it can.' 'Directs an action a single-prompt caller cannot take' is a judgement about the meaning of English prose; a Go test given the two strings cannot compute it. Whatever the implementer writes must therefore re-encode that judgement as literals — a list of directives, or a list of sentences — which is precisely the list-form §4.2.3 rejects and which test 19's own rationale says was 'short by one and had to be re-checked by hand'. The spec has rejected both available constructions and left the test with none. Two further inputs are unpinned and change the result: 'split into sentences' has no rule (the key contains an ellipsis, `§` tokens, `tp review` command strings and abbreviations, so a period-split and a prose-split disagree on the sentence set), and the comparison is exact-string or normalised is not said.
suggestion: Pick one constructible form and say so. The cheapest that keeps §4.2.3's property honest: assert the SET RELATION rather than the meaning — the `--role` instruction's sentence set is a proper subset of the unrestricted one, and it contains no occurrence of the four literal directive tokens the key can emit ('Agent tool', '--merge', '--record', '--perspective regression'), the token list being derived from `buildReviewLoopInstruction`'s own assignment sites rather than hand-written. Also fix the sentence-splitting rule (e.g. split on the emitted newline boundaries, not on '.').

finding: Test 19 was rewritten this round into a derived form, and the property it derives is strictly stronger than the rule §4.2.3 states, so an implementation that satisfies the spec can fail the test. §4.2.3's normative rule is a one-way implication: 'Under `--role`, no sentence of `review_loop.instruction` may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support.' It constrains only what may be KEPT. Test 19 asserts a biconditional over both directions: 'every sentence present without `--role` and absent with it directs an action a single-prompt caller cannot take, while every sentence kept is one it can.' The second clause is §4.2.3's rule; the first is a new requirement that nothing supportable may be dropped. Concretely, `buildReviewLoopInstruction` also emits the 'Read the spec at <path> before processing each prompt' sentence — an action a single-prompt caller CAN take, so §4.2.3 permits keeping it and is silent on dropping it, while test 19 fails any implementation that drops it. Second, both halves rest on the predicate 'directs an action a single-prompt caller cannot take', and §4.2.3 and test 19 each explicitly reject the only enumerable form of it (§4.2.3: 'not a list of sentences to delete'; test 19: 'A draft enumerated the forbidden directives instead'). Nothing in the spec supplies a computable classifier in its place, and test 19's own justification for rejecting the list — 'the list was short by one and had to be re-checked by hand' — is a report that a human made the call. The rule and its test therefore share an oracle the release does not define.
suggestion: Make test 19 assert §4.2.3's implication and nothing more: 'every sentence present with `--role` directs an action a single-prompt caller can take', plus a non-degeneracy assertion so an implementation that emits an empty string cannot pass (e.g. the `--role` key is non-empty and still names the spec path). Then give the predicate an operational form the test can evaluate — e.g. a sentence is unsupportable iff it names a `prompts[]` entry the payload does not contain, or a `tp review` mode §4.2.2 refuses to a `--role` caller — so the classifier is a property of the payload rather than a judgment. If no such form exists, say in §4.2.3 that the rule is reviewed by a human at decomposition and drop test 19's derived half rather than specifying a test that cannot be written.

finding: The release gate has no selector an implementer can code, and the two the spec does give disagree by 17 files. Test 14 states it as a runtime predicate — "every spec in `spec/` the repository can emit prompts for" — while §7's measured justification is stated over a different set: "22 version specs, 5 KB to 79 KB, 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none". Counted: `spec/` holds 39 `.md` files; exactly 22 match `^<major>.<minor>.<patch>.md$` and the remaining 17 (`0.11.0-review.md`, `0.16.0-review-orchestration.md`, `0.20.0-review-state.md`, `0.33.0-candidates.md`, `0.34.0-guard-tests.md`, `0.35.0-candidates.md`, …) are ordinary markdown tp can emit prompts for just as well. So the literal test-14 wording selects 39 and §7's argument holds only over 22, and nothing in the spec says which. Since §7 makes this the one gate that blocks the release, the difference is not cosmetic: under the literal reading 24 of the selected specs have no recorded round, which also widens the test-18 conflict.
suggestion: State the selector as a rule, not as a count: e.g. "every `spec/*.md` whose basename matches `^\\d+\\.\\d+\\.\\d+$` — 22 files today", and let the 15/7 split follow from it. Then §7's measured sentence and test 14's predicate name the same set and the test can compute it.

finding: §1.1's replacement for the deleted figure index states two commitments about the rest of the document, and the document falsifies both in the same round they were written. (1) 'every use elsewhere writes "suffix" or "net delta" next to the number, and a bare figure with neither word is the defect.' §6.2 test 5 reads 'the prompt with the clauses appended is exactly **467** bytes longer than the same prompt without them' — neither word, and it is the one site §1.1 names as its reason for writing the arithmetic out ('because §6.2 test 5 asserts it as an exact integer'). §1.1's own headline, '**467 bytes per role prompt.**', is the same form. (2) 'So there is no index.' §6.3 test 12 closes with '468 is the suffix; 467 is the net delta test 5 asserts. §1's table separates them.' — a two-entry index of which figure means what, one entry of which names another test by number, which is exactly the hand-maintained, drift-prone form §1.1 abolished one section earlier. The arithmetic itself is correct (measured from §2.2's and §3.2's verbatim strings: 287 + 177 bytes, 2 + 287 + 2 + 177 = 468 suffix, 467 net), so the defect is entirely in the labelling discipline the section just adopted.
suggestion: Label test 5's figure — 'exactly **467** bytes longer, the net delta of §1.1's table' — and delete test 12's trailing index sentence, since test 12 already writes 'the 468-byte suffix' one clause earlier and no longer needs to disambiguate. Optionally label §1.1's own headline ('net delta: 467 bytes per role prompt') so the rule holds inside the section that states it.

finding: §1.1's third attempt at an anti-drift rule for 467/468 is stated as a testable defect predicate — 'every use elsewhere writes "suffix" or "net delta" next to the number, and a bare figure with neither word is the defect' — and the current document violates it at three sites, one of which is the sentence that introduces the table stating the rule. Every occurrence: line 32 '**467 bytes per role prompt.**' (bare, and it is §1.1's own headline); line 47 'the net change to the body is 467' (says 'net change', not the required 'net delta'); line 573, §6.2 test 5, 'exactly **467** bytes longer' (bare — and this is the one test that asserts the integer, so it is the site where the rule most matters). Compliant sites are lines 44, 546 and 606. No numbered test owns the rule, so nothing in §6 can fail when it is broken — which is how the two preceding versions of this same guard (round 7's 'refers back to this table' and round 8's section registry) were each reported broken the round after they were written.
suggestion: Either make it mechanical or drop it. Mechanical: add it to §6 as an assertion over the spec text (every occurrence of 467 or 468 in `spec/0.36.0.md` outside §1.1's table is within N characters of the literal 'suffix' or 'net delta'), and fix the three violations first so the rule ships green. Otherwise delete the rule sentence and let the table stand alone — a fourth prose guard is a fourth thing to drift.

finding: §4.2.1's skip table is presented as the complete taxonomy of non-emission — §6.3 test 9 reads it that way ('Each of the five skip reasons in §4.2.1's table is exercised') and §4.2.1's exit-0/exit-2 dichotomy is built on it — and §4.1's paragraph added this round documents a sixth non-emission the table does not carry. §4.1 now says regression is appended 'From round 2 onward, when the spec has changed or findings were resolved fixed', and explains the round-3 row as 'the absence of the trigger… neither half of the condition above held and `regression` was not appended'. The table's only regression row is `no-baseline` annotated '(`regression` at round 1)'. Confirmed in the emitter: buildReviewPrompts appends regression under `!noState && round >= 2 && (diffBlock != "" || len(fixed) > 0)` (internal/cli/review.go:871-883), while the `SkipNoBaseline` entry is written to `skipped` only under `round < 2` (line 907-908). So at round >= 2 with no diff and no fixed finding — §4.1's own round-3 row — regression is in neither `prompts[]` nor `skipped_roles`, and `--role regression` there is recognised (a built-in, so not exit 2) with no `skipped_roles` entry (so not exit 0 as §4.2.1 specifies). The release's worked example for the exit-0 rule is the one role whose most common non-emission the table omits.
suggestion: Add the sixth condition to §4.2.1's table as its own row — regression at round >= 2 with no spec change and no fixed finding, which drops the prompt, is never a unit, and carries NO reason — and say which branch §4.2.1 assigns it (it must be exit 0, since the name is a built-in). Then either have the emitter record a reason for it so `skipped_roles` stays the complete account of non-emission, or state in §4.2.1 that the exit-0 branch does not require a `skipped_roles` entry. Update test 9's 'five skip reasons' accordingly and give test 7 a case at round >= 2 without a trigger, which is the state §4.1 measured and no test covers.

finding: Test 16 fixes its iteration set as 'For each unit `BuildNextUnits` returns, execute its `brief_command` and assert exit 0', but never pins the fixture's PHASE, and `BuildNextUnits` is the driver's general unit builder over spec/0.35.0's eight unit kinds — not a role-unit enumerator. The clause that follows ('under a fixture where a corpus role is skipped `no-checklist-items`') describes the corpus, not the phase, so one engineer builds a review-phase fixture and iterates two role units while another runs it against a tree whose phase yields `implement` or `decompose` units and executes their briefs. That second reading is not merely broader, it is destructive and undetected: an `implement` unit's brief is `tp next --brief`, which CLAIMS a task and writes the task file — and test 18, the suite's only isolation assertion, hashes `spec/.tp-review/` and `.tp/rounds/` only, so a suite that mutates `<base>.tasks.json` reports green. This release changes `BriefCommand` for `review-role` and `audit-role` only (§4.2.3), so the wide reading also tests briefs the release does not touch.
suggestion: Scope test 16 to the kinds the release changes: 'for each `review-role` and `audit-role` unit `BuildNextUnits` returns, under a review-phase and an audit-phase fixture respectively'. If the wider iteration is wanted, extend §6.1's outcome (and test 18's hash) to cover the task file so a brief that claims a task cannot pass unnoticed.

finding: Test 19 asserts a biconditional that §4.2.3's rule does not require, so an implementation that fully satisfies the spec can fail the test. §4.2.3 fixes one direction only: 'Under `--role`, no sentence of `review_loop.instruction` may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support' — i.e. nothing unsupportable may REMAIN. Test 19 additionally requires that 'every sentence kept is one it can [take]', i.e. nothing supportable may be DROPPED. A conformant implementation that drops one harmless-but-pointless sentence (say the one naming the spec path twice) violates test 19 while violating no clause of §4.2.3. Since §4.2.3 is the section that decides what the release must do and §6.4 is what decides whether it did, the acceptance is stricter than the requirement and the difference is not stated anywhere.
suggestion: Either widen §4.2.3's rule to the biconditional it means ('a sentence is present under `--role` if and only if the single-prompt caller can act on it') or narrow test 19 to §4.2.3's single direction and say explicitly that dropping a supportable sentence is permitted.

finding: §1.1's round-9 rewrite retires the hand-maintained figure index (correctly — it had drifted) and replaces it with a per-use annotation rule: "every use elsewhere writes 'suffix' or 'net delta' next to the number, and a bare figure with neither word is the defect." Measured against the document it governs, the rule is already violated at the one site that matters most. The five 467/468 uses outside §1.1 are: line 546 (§6.1's property, "§1's 468-byte suffix" — labelled), line 605 and line 606 (§6.3 test 12, "the 468-byte suffix" and "468 is the suffix; 467 is the net delta" — labelled), and line 573, §6.2 test 5: "exactly **467** bytes longer than the same prompt without them" — bare, with neither word. Test 5 is the assertion the whole table exists to protect and the one place a transcription error becomes a compiled constant. §1.1's own opening line 32 ("**467 bytes per role prompt.**") is bare too, though it sits in the deriving section. So the third mechanism in three rounds for the same two constants is unenforced by anything and is not obeyed by the round that wrote it — which is the same failure mode as the index it replaced, one indirection later.
suggestion: Either write "net delta" into test 5 this round (a two-word edit that makes the rule true), or drop the annotation rule and stop stating 468 at all: the suffix is fully determined by "the two clause strings plus two LF LF separators" and the net delta by "that, minus the stripped trailing newline", so §6.1's property and test 12 can both be phrased without an integer, leaving exactly one literal in the document — the one test 5 asserts.
